nameStory: The Brown Funnel Polypore gets its name from its distinctive funnel or vase-like shape that develops as it matures. Unlike many mushrooms that start funnel-shaped and flatten out, this one does the opposite - beginning relatively flat and deepening into a pronounced funnel over time. The 'polypore' part refers to its underside, which has tiny pores instead of gills.
description: The Brown Funnel Polypore is a distinctive bracket fungus that looks like a small, woody funnel attached to a slender stem. These tough, leathery mushrooms typically measure 1-3 inches across with caps that range from rusty brown to cinnamon colored with darker concentric zones. They're perennial fungi, meaning the same fruiting body can persist and grow for multiple years, becoming increasingly funnel-shaped and weathered over time. You'll often find them growing in small clusters from sandy soil or decaying wood.

idTips.label: Cap Shape
idTips.description: Starts nearly flat but develops into a deep funnel or vase shape with age. The center becomes so depressed it almost looks like a small wooden bowl with concentric ridges.

idTips.label: Cap Color
idTips.description: Rich brown to cinnamon colored with darker brown concentric zones that create a target-like pattern. Feels dry and velvety when young, becoming tough and leathery.

idTips.label: Pores
idTips.description: Underside has tiny angular pores (not gills) that are yellowish-brown to rusty brown. The pore surface extends down the stem, and pokes feel firm to the touch.

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Slender, tough, and darker brown than the cap. Often slightly fuzzy or velvety, especially toward the base. Feels woody and inflexible when bent.

idTips.label: Spore Print
idTips.description: Produces a white to pale yellow spore print. Place the cap pore-side down on paper overnight to see this diagnostic feature.

habitat: Look for Brown Funnel Polypores in sandy, acidic soils in pine and mixed coniferous forests throughout New England. They're particularly common along hiking trails, in clearings, and at forest edges where the soil is well-drained. You'll often spot them growing from buried wood, old stumps, or directly from the forest floor in areas with decomposing organic matter.

seasonality.spring: Old fruiting bodies from previous years become more noticeable as snow melts, appearing weathered and grayish. New growth may begin in late spring during warm, wet periods.
seasonality.summer: Fresh, vibrant brown caps emerge and develop their characteristic funnel shape. This is prime time for finding specimens with the classic velvety texture and rich coloration.
seasonality.fall: Mature fruiting bodies reach peak development, with deep funnel shapes clearly visible. Colors may fade slightly but the tough texture helps them persist through early frosts.
seasonality.winter: Older specimens become weathered and grayish but remain attached and identifiable. The woody texture allows them to survive freezing temperatures, though they become more brittle.

funFact: These remarkable fungi can live for several years, with the same fruiting body adding new growth layers each season like tree rings - some specimens found in New England have been tracked growing in the exact same spot for over five years!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other brown bracket fungi, but the distinctive funnel shape and ground-growing habit set it apart. Remember: 'Funnel from the forest floor' - if it's deeply funnel-shaped and growing from soil rather than obviously from a tree trunk, it's likely your Brown Funnel Polypore.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'polypore,' this fungus belongs to a different family than most bracket fungi you see on trees. The name can be misleading since many people associate polypores only with tree-growing species, but this ground-dwelling exception proves fungi don't always follow our naming expectations.
compareHints: The Brown Funnel Polypore differs from its cousin the Shiny Cinnamon Polypore by its deeper funnel shape and less glossy surface texture. While Shiny Cinnamon Polypore tends to stay relatively flat with a more lacquered appearance, Brown Funnel Polypore develops that distinctive deep depression and maintains a more matte, velvety finish. Both grow from soil, but the funnel shape is the dead giveaway for this species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its closest relative, the brown funnel polypore (Coltricia perennis), the shiny cinnamon polypore is much glossier when fresh and tends to be more shelf-like rather than funnel-shaped.
